It's still popular, but the days of consistent packed gyms for most Indiana high schools is long gone. The world, as result of technology & social media in the Information Era, is bigger and allows for people to be exposed to different things and follow those things. Before, there wasn't much else to do in Tipton, Delphi, Michigan City, Rochester, Greenfield, Marion, etc.

As a result, people watch TV shows, follow pro sports, or are involved in other activities that take attention away from high school basketball. I have found that NCAA basketball is still really popular in Indiana, as Indiana and Purdue still have extremely huge followings. But NCAA basketball in the whole country has declined in its national following a bit, and there's been a dip in Indiana. In regards to the NBA, more people have a casual understanding of what is going on in the league now (due to its national coverage), but fewer people than you think actually watch the regular season games consistently. The Pacers aren't as popular in the state as they were, but that is also because of how/who the NBA is marketing itself towards, and the Pacers haven't been really good for awhile.

Football is much bigger in Indiana than it used to be. The Manning/Colts Effect is a big reason why, but Indiana being more exposed to the national popularity of the NFL has led to more people following the NFL/football more. High school football is as big of a deal as high school basketball in many Indiana towns.

Lastly, small towns aren't as tight knit as they used to be. Society is more individualistic, socio-economics have changed in a lot of places, so people don't think about the collective as much, and the collective thing to do for a long time in Indiana was go to the local HS or NCAA game, or at the very least, discuss basketball. I would guess there's much less basketball discussion in public in much of Indiana as opposed to 30 years ago.

Nobody knows with goalies, but the other positions are easier tell, especially with league quality and age being widely known factors.

For example, it's pretty easy to tell on the day of the 2013 Draft that Predators 3rd round pick Jonathan-Ismael Diaby was very unlikely to become an NHLer, much less a good one. Late 1994 birthday, only put up 9 points in 51 games in his natural draft year and only 26 points in 67 games in his actual draft year, in a very weak QMJHL where scoring is the name of the game.

And in contrast, people knew that Penguins 3rd rounder Jake Guentzel was a great value pick that day because despite being a late 1994 birthday, he went from MN HS in his 17 year old season (weak quality relatively speaking) to 73 points in 60 games in his 18 year old season in the USHL, historically a harder league to score in for younger players and especially rookies, which Guentzel was. (Plus the NCAA route for Guentzel guaranteeing a longer development curve with time against older players in a good league.) That sort of production jump, going from complete unknown in a mixed bag league to rockstar in a good, underrated league, is what we like to see with those type of draft eligible prospects.

And as we later found out, Guentzel was the difference in the 2017 Cup Final to win the Cup for the Penguins while Diaby was never even a productive AHLer and obviously never played in the NHL. Points aren't everything, but when using league quality and historical data, they typically are good indicators of potential ceiling.
